S1sw:
The New Age May Dawn Suddenly

I just put a movie my father made in 1988 up on the Internet for the first time: Where's Utopia? It was the result of years of work, traveling to all kinds of communes and communal experiments around the country, trying to answer a question that for him was primary: How do we live together without recreating the same loneliness, domination, and stupidity we were supposedly escaping?

He had already spent 17 years in the Bruderhof, a Christian community that doesn’t use money internally. He had no personal money there: income went into the common purse and the community provided what members needed. So when I talk later about moving beyond internal money, I’m not proposing something nobody has ever lived. My father spent most of two decades doing it. They also accepted him as a Jewish atheist, making him a remarkably long-running doctrinal exception. In meditation there, he came to his own understanding that “God is the Universe, and the Universe is Love.”

[caption] This was the banner my mom painted that hung in our living room for decades. I will try to locate the actual photo.

He might have stayed, but the U.S. antiwar movement during Vietnam needed somebody who knew how to set up printing presses. He eventually founded the Aquarian Research Foundation—not a commune, but a nonprofit devoted to researching how the planet could have a positive future and publishing what it found. His conclusion was simple and enormous: human beings need small tribal communities again, because Civilization Is A Hoax, as I blogged about at the beginning of the Covid plandemic.

That’s where the escuelita in my title comes in. Escuelita means “little school.” I’m borrowing the word from the Zapatistas in Mexico, whose Escuelita brought outsiders into their communities for a while to learn autonomy by living it. In the same way, people would live in the healing communities I’m proposing, to heal and to learn the relational and practical methods, so that some of them could eventually leave and set up another one somewhere else. Otherwise, we’ve built a lovely refuge for whoever got there first.

I spent much of my childhood being carried through Twin Oaks, Acorn, East Wind, Padanaram, Zendik, and many other communities. I was usually just a visitor’s kid, close enough to see how people lived but never quite part of the tribe. At the time that meant a lot of boredom, with some adventures mixed in, but those years gave me a great sample to compare against.

From 1999 to 2001, my family actually lived with the Love Israel family in Washington while escaping Y2K, that brief historical period when otherwise reasonable adults prepared for civilization to be defeated by a two-digit date. We lived in a yurt. There were wild berries of every kind, and I loved being in nature. I was also lonely, bored, irritated by the cult programming, and missing my friends in Philadelphia.

I wanted to befriend the children there, but they treated me as an outsider. My mom never liked the place. The leader was also named Love Israel, and to me he seemed like the fakest person I’d ever met, complete with the expected God complex.

We spent a lot of time on our knees in the community garden growing food they could sell in town. The money was opaque and seemed to travel mostly upward toward Love. Meanwhile everybody sang, “Here in the garden, there’s nothing left to do but eat sleep and keep clean.” Again and again. 🌱

My father eventually gave the community his airplane. They sold it instead of using it. He felt tricked, began exposing what was happening, and then we were asked to leave.

The East Wind commune was almost the opposite way. There were maybe eighty people when I was there, enough to have a variety of personalities, small enough to actually make friends. I was happy there. I especially liked showering in a communal shower with both sexes present. I wonder if that still goes on at East Wind? It's the sort of thing that doesn't make it into the history books.

Even at East Wind, though, there was a quieter power issue. They had a nut butter factory that brought in a lot of their income, which seemed to make the woman running it very hard to question. Otherwise I thought the community had a great social life, a nice way of distributing labor, and no obvious guru.

There were like eight people at Acorn when I was there, and no kids. I couldn't tell whether it was a commune I might join or a group of people who were already friends, and who happened to live on some really beautiful land and be good at building cool stuff. Joining would have felt less like applying to a commune than asking whether their group chat had an opening.

Twin Oaks was much bigger, like two or three hundred people at the time, and almost institutional. It was friendly and interesting, but I didn't feel like I was in a tribe there. It was more like a tiny hippie town, but with a highly structured political system that didn't seem intuitive for hippies.

Looking back, almost none of these communities had a communal therapy practice. People brought the usual human pain and suffering with them, and it all got translated into politics.

Which meant weekly meetings, run according to Robert's Rules of Order, with enormous agendas, where most of the things you needed to talk about couldn't be talked about, and you generally felt like you'd rather be sleeping. (Some people, including me, solved this problem by just going to sleep in the meeting and openly snoring.)

Zendik went in the other direction. They held a brutal community meeting that I’m still recovering from 35 years later. 🤣 Five-year-old me was put in the center and told I was bad because I hadn’t volunteered to help adults with whatever jobs they were doing. Apparently kindergarten had already failed to teach me labor consciousness.

The secular communities often buried hurt under procedure. The spiritual communities often put one person in charge of everybody’s inner life. Most of the rest of this article is my attempt to describe the missing third option.

S8v30:
The Grown Children Get the Final Review

Couples who live together, share the same culture and even the same bed still disagree about screens, vaccinations, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. And that's just two people. Now think of twenty adults, all with different childhoods.

The community has to share enough principles about raising kids to offer them coherence, and leave parents enough room to remain parents.

My own childhood broke many mainstream rules about what children should see and do. I won’t unpack all of it here. I’m grateful that my mother nursed me until I was five, grateful my parents didn’t vaccinate me, and grateful for nearly all of the unusual world they gave me.

[caption] Me as a child, wearing the pen holder my dad made, ready to write my Final Review 😹

I mention vaccination specifically because it's one of the values I would absolutely need to share with people in a community, if I was going to raise children there. I'm not trying to design a village for everyone, only saying that communities need some common ground among the parents on children's health, enough that they can actually trust one another.

All of the community's design and implementation will ultimately be reviewed by the kids, once they're grown, and their review weighs more heavily than founders usually want it to. Adults can go on about their intentions forever, but those grown kids who lived through the system as it actually manifested might have another perspective.

I actually learned how to parent my son from his future review via his quantum jumping time machine, which he explained in this video:

Double click to interact with video

A friend who reviewed this draft grew up in a Christian commune in Colorado where her father was a pastor. She calls her childhood "a treasure and a burden." A treasure because she belonged and everybody cared for everybody. A burden because of the strict religious life she never chose.

What she said is more useful than the usual promo video showing kids smiling and carrying vegetables.

Communal Parenting Adds On

One of the biggest reasons I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept. It's one outsider's interpretation of the Ye'kuana, an Indigenous people of the Venezuelan rainforest she lived with, and she may have idealized what she saw, but it's still a powerful picture: the babies are carried along in ordinary adult life, the kids are surrounded by people of several ages and learn by taking part, and it doesn't fall on one exhausted parent to be a child's whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.

Experiments where kids sleep and live apart from their parents deserve special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that the practice of kids sleeping communally eventually ended for a mix of reasons: developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. Kids can benefit from high-quality group care and multiple loving adults in their lives, but replacing a secure attachment to their parents is a different matter.

Tamera's Children's Place has repeated some of these old Kibbutz failings, taking children away from biological parents, because their founders' ideology said that children are traumatized by the nuclear family and its unstable romantic underpinnings. On the other hand, their actual practice did allow parents (including fathers) to stay with their children in Children's Place, so they weren't as dogmatic as I originally thought. My own bias is still toward a system where kids are not solely taken care of by their parents, while still honoring the parent-child bond. If the father is unknown, the whole community can do the fathering, but the biological mom's role should always be honored, since that attachment is formed already from years of nursing.

Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection

[caption] African kids enjoying their childhood!

Kids also need their own territory, places where they can create their own society, invent games and work out ordinary disputes, without always being under the management of adults.

I got a taste of that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it's still one of the freest memories I have. ZEGG's Kinderhaus works from a similar intuition. Adults take care of safety on the outside, but kids still get a world of their own.

This could be badly misunderstood, so the safeguards need to be explicit. The adults still have to pay attention to what goes on in a children's territory. Older kids can't be allowed to quietly boss the younger ones around there. And keeping secrets can't be treated as independence.

I also reject the suburban panic that treats every warm relationship between a child and an unrelated adult as suspicious. It's good for kids to have a whole bunch of grownups who know them and enjoy them, who would notice when something changes, and who would act when something's wrong. When adults panic like that, kids can lose all those grownups without the panic actually preventing abuse.

There are several parts to this protection:

Give children real agency. When kids say no, it counts. No grownup has a right to their affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.

Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it's about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. A surprise has an end date. But secrets meant to isolate a kid aren't allowed.

Protecting children is the duty of adults, but it requires children to help also. "The Boy Who Cried Wolf" is a didactic children's story which continues to be useful generation after generation. The Buddha even taught his son honesty as the most important first lesson. I agree. We must teach children truthfulness before there's a crisis. "Make believe" must be labeled as such. When adults lie to children (like Santa is real etc), that teaches them to misunderstand the difference between reality and make-believe. Make sure kids understand what they say will be taken seriously if they are known to be honest. Don't let the teaching turn into interrogation or punishment when they're not sure. A scared or confused kid may get mixed up telling what happened and still need protection.

Hear the child even when the accused is someone people love. Communities fail here, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or everybody's friend. Decide on the response process ahead of time, before anyone's face is attached to it. Keep everyone at risk safe first, right away, then make sure the accusation is investigated competently and fairly. Nobody's status buys silence.

Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. Make sure there's at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route they can reach without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities raided a religious community in Island Pond and took 112 kids into custody over suspected abuse. A judge turned down the state's blanket request to hold them, because it couldn't name any specific case, and the kids went home that same day. State intervention can fail spectacularly, and enclosing kids completely in a community can fail too. Kids need more than one world.

Sometimes we also need to protect people from the rare, but real threat posed by dangerous children. I looked through the research corpus for a well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to others. I was looking to find the reported conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I couldn't find one. It's possible that records are private, or that cases were referred elsewhere. Whatever the reason, I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest cases on their own. In those cases, the child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review, hopefully including non-intrusive help from outside the home community.

The Door Must Open Outward at Adulthood

If a community's kids never leave, it has no way of knowing whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel and make friends, encounter other ways of living, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors. And kids coming back isn't necessarily the best thing for the communal movement either. If they then start their own communities, we may see more evolution than if they simply return and continue what their parents started.

Amish young people, age 16, go through a 2-year period of freedom from parental control called Rumspringa. During this time they might travel outside, although they normally choose to stay in the community and begin acting as adults, including courtship. At the end of this period, they decide as adults whether to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more of them end up joining. Pop culture makes Rumspringa seem like a wilder, more universal teenage free-for-all than it is, but the main point is that they're baptized as adults, which means belonging is a commitment they make.

Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary parents aren't going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, "Go see the world." They'll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work, so they can become self-sufficient, and eventually take care of their aging parents. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and basic survival may rightly come first.

Unlimited freedom isn't realistic, but it doesn't need to be artificially impossible for grown kids to leave. Kids in or outside of intentional communities all need to learn enough about how the money world outside operates that they aren't helpless in it. Like how to get a job, pay rent, read contracts, handle banks, get IDs, avoid getting scammed, and how to ask for help when they're unsure about any of that. And all that sounds amorphous if it's not structured into plausible next steps outside the community (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, another community).

Kids also need transferable skills and education. It helps if they have relationships with people outside the community. They should be able to access their own records and documents. It would be great if the community could also provide resources to smooth the transition, like temporary housing, help with travel, etc.

Belonging and freedom should go hand in hand.
S12v14:
The Math of Absorption, and Who This Isn’t For

Many perfectly intelligent grownups would rather sit around for six hours talking about solar panels than talk about jealousy, God, death, childhood, money, sex, psychedelics, or somebody wanting to leave, which is what I ask people to do in this article.

This doesn't surprise me, since we're taught to put on a show of competence in modern society. We're given a lot of incentives to hide ourselves and disappear behind our screens the second things get uncomfortable. Emotional intelligence doesn't pay the bills. Instead we optimize to fit the career market with all the little energy we've got. A new study found that where relationships are easy to make and break, people even feel less on the same page with whoever doesn't help them reach their goals. Kind of a "no, duh" study, but still.

So then a lot of people end up thinking they aren't "good enough" for community, or getting labeled by others that way. And there's a real issue there, but it's more about what fits where & when than good or bad. The community needs to consider how much attention the newcomer currently has available for other people, how willing they are to examine their own reactions. And on the other hand, look at whether the group has enough free resource/capacity to support them without becoming a full-time caretaker operation.

Some people have engaged in long practices of contemplation or therapy, or have had very good luck in childhood; other people are just trying to survive some emergency in their life and need care more than responsibility. Most of us are all of these at different times in our lives.

In the model I’m imagining, some of the functions that are outsourced to therapists in modern society are distributed throughout the community. In other words, there’s a lot of peer counseling going on, people listening to each other, being there for each other and helping each other process ordinary emotional stuff.

That does not make the community infinitely absorbent like a Heavy Flow Maxi Pad.

I’m going to use the phrase “free resource,” which comes from Re-evaluation Counseling, to refer to the attention, steadiness, skill and practical capacity people have left over for others once they’ve dealt with enough of their own immediate stuff, and “need” to refer to the amount of help people need at a given time.

Everyone has a certain amount of both in different ratios.

My own need has exceeded my free resource at many points. Good Lord. During one stretch, my first wife tried to kill me while psychotic because she believed I was her sociopathic father. Then she took my son. Later she tried to kill my mother, while her pimp stalked my sister’s family until they moved to Canada.

I could go on and on, but the math is pretty clear by now. There wasn’t much of me left over for anybody else. So when I say someone might need to stabilize and do inner pl/ork before helping found a community, I’m not saying it from a mountaintop.

The ability to welcome somebody is partly a problem of resources, then, not compassion -- how many people can a group take in without hurting the existing members or the people they are taking in?

And that also brings us to a difficult catch-22 for fledgling groups. The need for new members in a small community is greater, but the ability of that community to absorb disruption is less. With only eight people in the community, someone still has to grow the food and fix whatever breaks. Somebody has to balance the books and watch the kids. And the water system has to keep working. The water well doesn’t care how beautiful the new member’s heart is.

So early on, members usually need to have more available resource than acute need, and some practical skills to contribute. They usually need to be willing to learn, too. Once there are 80 members, though, there's usually a lot more free resource to draw on.

I still don’t know how to keep this language of capacity from becoming a respectable way to exclude people who are disabled, poor, less articulate, maybe simply uncomfortable or unfamiliar with therapeutic language, or for whatever reason deemed inconvenient. Pretending capacity is unlimited won’t solve that. Any real process would need concrete criteria, review by someone who wasn’t part of the decision, and a way to revisit a “not now” decision on membership. Even then, the power to veto membership applications based on capacity remains dangerously tilted towards elitism.

But before you submit your application to the community, submit it to yourself. This community may not be a good fit for you right now if:

You have a need that far outstrips your free resource right now. This doesn’t mean you’re bad or doomed, it’s about timing; it just means you need to take a first step of finding support where you are and building up your resources. If you don't have a free resource calculator on hand, an easy way to tell is if you’re running from some crisis right now and mainly need a place to land, get treatment, housing, legal aid, etc. A founding group shouldn’t pretend it can give you those.

You want the feeling of village life but don’t want to take on governance, maintenance, conflict, care, etc.

You’re not willing to look at yourself when jealousy or conflict comes up.

Any humane membership process should have ways of not flat-out rejecting people who fall into these categories, or anyone else it can’t take right now, like saying “later,” or “in another role,” or “with more support.”
S15v13:
What This Looks Like From Sénégal

The “African Renaissance Monument” in Dakar, Sénégal, which stands at 160 feet tall and took 4 years to build.

I live in Sénégal, where "intentional community" often sounds like a strange Western phrase. People here are like, "Don't human beings already do that?"

Sénégal is unlike anywhere else I've lived. Five times a day the prayers pour out into the streets. I find them so soothing! And Sufism doesn't stay inside designated "spiritual" places here. It's in the music, in the pictures everywhere, in the murals, in the names, in the conversations.

And the humor! People are outside laughing for hours at a time. This is the most joking culture I've ever been in, and I keep wondering if I'll ever understand the really complicated jokes in Wolof. Basic conversation is one thing. But knowing why twelve people are suddenly crying with laughter? That's graduate school.

In the villages and families I've spent time around, so much is taken care of by the extended family and the local memory, alongside the formal systems. Whether it's land, childcare, housing, food, obligations, etc, etc. Who needs a workshop called "Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging" when some aunt has already given three people a task?

Even in Dakar, I found this graffiti on a wall: "Tolerance! Openness! Union! Happiness! Love!" And elsewhere there are murals of Sufi leaders. Spiritual graffiti still surprises me! Where I grew up, a city wall was either selling you a product or showing off somebody's inability to draw a penis.

Graffiti in Dakar, Sénégal: Tolerance! Openness! Union! Happiness! Love!

All is not well in paradise

But does this mean I think Sénégal is some magical place that's kept its communal paradise? No, not that either! The warmth has hard limits here, and LGBTQ+ people can pay a brutal price for crossing them.

Sénégal passed a law in March 2026 (Law No. 2026-08) that increased the penalty for consensual same-sex intimacy to 5 to 10 years in prison, and it also made public advocacy for homosexuality a crime. Homosexuals were already facing arrests, family rejection, harassment, assault and mob violence, but some say they're actually protected once they're arrested, because then at least the mob can't get at them. I'm not going to praise communal belonging and ignore the people who have to hide who they are to survive it, or leave.

So which is it? Well, in a way, it's both. It's possible for a society to be spiritually alive, generous, funny and super communal, while still becoming cruel to those who break its social categories. It's interesting to see that being in community isn't necessarily liberating for everyone, it all depends on whether you're allowed to belong without pretending.

One other shadow side of the otherwise forgiving social culture here is that people may go to great lengths to avoid confrontation. Who stole the sheep? We all know, but nobody wants to cause a stink by bringing it up.

Where I live, neighbors steal our moringa pods every morning. Every morning! They could plant a moringa tree in their own yard. Apparently maintaining this relationship with ours is more entertaining. 😂

Everybody here has sheep (even me!), and they are super cute! It can feel like you're living in another world, with the music, the animals, the joking, the praying, and just being around people all the time.

Of course, the old communal ways here are changing. Young people move to the city, get a job, get a phone, eat imported food, become part of the wider world, etc. (some of the men even make the dangerous journey by sea to Europe). So what about the families? The ones that used to share almost everything are now more reliant on cash and individual opportunities.

Lessons from the Black Tax

Then there's the so-called "Black Tax," a strange legacy of the old communal system: if you've got any money at all, you're expected to share it with your parents, your siblings, your cousins, to pay school fees, medical bills, funerals, etc. I understand the instinct. In the ancestral way of doing things nobody made it alone, and the people who fed and raised you had a real claim on whatever you made of yourself later. So why not share in return? That's how the whole organism survived (it wasn't charity).

But these days it can be soul destroying. People have a lot less of the communal life that held the obligation up (the shared land, work, childcare, food and daily belonging), but they still carry it. So if one of them makes it into the cash economy, it's really hard to build any independence or long-term stability, because they may be expected to carry everybody. How can they get ahead, when all these people are dependent on them? And the relatives stay dependent too, since the payments don't give them a real alternative. It's the ancestral ethic playing out inside an individualistic cash economy. It can keep people alive, but it eats away at both sides too.

This is also the thorny boundary issue of living without money inside a money-based society. Life inside the commune can go without cash, but you'll still need money for taxes, hospital bills, visas, school fees, family obligations, buying in tools etc. That doesn't mean going back to individual wages inside the commune, but it does mean someone has to handle it! Who's that going to be? And the commune has to work out how much shared cash it keeps for these things, and how to stop access to outside money from creating a new status hierarchy.

Another aspect of outside work, even before there's a common purse, is that it's not just money you're bringing into the commune. You're also bringing in a different schedule, a different status system, a different social world, different loyalties, and often different consumption habits etc. etc. And you can't exactly leave all that at the door, can you? In the first stage, where people working outside should contribute an agreed share, it's really important that they can't use the money to buy their way out of everyday communal work, or to buy a greater say in the political system. It's also important that the group notices when outside jobs start draining the people and skills it needs to build the communal livelihoods. Otherwise the commune will stay a dormitory for the money economy instead of moving toward a common purse.

Some Zapatista communities used to try to stop their young people from leaving, which is a version of the same outside-work problem. Now they talk it through with them instead: it's OK to go and work elsewhere, as long as the migrants keep certain defined obligations to the community. That doesn't make the pull between leaving and belonging go away, but at least now it's something they can name and negotiate. I understand the motivation to negotiate like that, but I think it's not a full solution either.

Westerners often start out isolated and try to rebuild a tribe. A lot of Africans start out with a communal life they inherited, and watch parts of it fall apart. Kind of the opposite problem, isn't it? And urban Africans who get interested in intentional community might come to it feeling alienated from both the city and the tradition they left.

So this is a global issue, far from some Western lifestyle niche. There's still knowledge in the living villages that no book can give you. But if you visit, remember they're people, not museums. Would you like people coming to your house to stare at you and your family? So be respectful, contribute something, learn the language, and don't expect anyone to hand you a spiritual service package!

Oh, and a practical note: getting my residency in Sénégal was pretty cheap and straightforward. French and Wolof matter a lot more than English. And the country's famous ideal of Teranga (hospitality) is real in my life. I'm staying in a friend's family's house, and they won't let me pay rent! Can you believe it? Of course that generosity lives right alongside watchfulness, social conservatism, bureaucracy and all the usual complications of a real country.
